flashcards.q: What is the core federation pattern behind SSO?
flashcards.a: An Identity Provider (IdP) asserts identity, and a Service Provider (SP) trusts that signed assertion instead of running its own login -- authenticate once at the IdP, access many SPs.

flashcards.q: What is the 2026 pragmatic rule of thumb for choosing SAML vs OIDC?
flashcards.a: OIDC is the default for new builds; SAML is used only when a legacy enterprise IdP (ADFS, older Okta/Ping deployments) forces it. Most B2B platforms support both behind one abstraction and let the customer's IdP dictate the choice.

flashcards.q: Quantify the performance difference between SAML and OIDC.
flashcards.a: OIDC ID tokens run ~1KB vs SAML's multi-KB XML assertions. Reported throughput advantage for OIDC is ~2.9-3.0x on a fixed CPU budget, with the verification-side gap reported as high as ~12x in some benchmarks, driven by XML canonicalization being a documented CPU sink.

flashcards.q: What is XML Signature Wrapping and why is it SAML-specific rather than a JWT risk?
flashcards.a: XML's structural flexibility lets an attacker inject unsigned nodes alongside a validly-signed node; a parser not strict about which node the signature actually covers can be tricked into trusting attacker content. JWT's flat 3-segment format (header.payload.signature) has no equivalent structural ambiguity -- one payload, one signature covering exactly it.

flashcards.q: What do SPIFFE and SPIRE each provide?
flashcards.a: SPIFFE standardizes the identity FORMAT (a spiffe://trust-domain/path URI plus an SVID document, typically X.509). SPIRE is the reference RUNTIME that attests workloads (verifies via node/workload attestation, not a shared secret) and issues short-lived SVIDs.

flashcards.q: What concretely breaks with a static long-lived API key that SPIFFE/SPIRE fixes?
flashcards.a: A static key has no natural rotation, is hard to audit (who still holds a copy?), and a leak grants standing indefinite access until manually noticed and rotated. SVIDs have hours-long TTLs, auto-rotated, so a leak's blast radius is bounded by construction, not by detection speed.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between TLS and mTLS?
flashcards.a: Standard TLS authenticates only the server to the client. Mutual TLS (mTLS) adds the reverse: the server also requests and verifies a client certificate, so both sides cryptographically prove identity before data flows.

flashcards.q: Does mTLS alone give you 'zero trust' networking?
flashcards.a: No -- mTLS gives strong mutual authentication only. Zero trust also requires per-request authorization decisions based on the verified identity (e.g., SPIFFE ID), not implicit trust because a call originated 'inside the mesh'.

flashcards.q: How does Istio provide SPIFFE-compliant identity by default?
flashcards.a: Istiod's built-in CA issues X.509-SVIDs natively for every service in the mesh by default; organizations wanting centralized certificate governance can configure Istiod to delegate to an external SPIRE deployment for a unified PKI hierarchy and audit trail.

flashcards.q: What operational risk does hourly SVID rotation introduce compared to yearly certificate rotation?
flashcards.a: A rotation pipeline failure tolerable at a yearly cadence (days to notice/fix) causes an outage within HOURS at an hourly cadence, since there's far less slack before expired identities fail mTLS handshakes. Requires genuinely automated, battle-tested rotation tooling and SPIRE control-plane availability as a Tier-1 SLO.
